findings.body:
Switching `subprocess.run` to `shell=True` with an f-string turns `upload_dir`, `name`, and `oid` into shell syntax. A crafted `name` or `oid` (for example `x; id > /tmp/pwned; #`) executes arbitrary commands as the service user and can write outside `/srv/thumbs/`.

ImageMagick policy delegates do not need a shell — keep the argv list (and the absolute binary path). If the upstream validator was the safety rail, it is no longer documented here and does not cover `upload_dir` / `oid` anyway.

```suggestion
    subprocess.run(
        ["/usr/bin/convert", f"{upload_dir}/{name}", f"/srv/thumbs/{oid}.png"],
        check=True,
    )
```

summary:
## Verdict

Critical command-injection regression in `make_thumb`: the conversion call was switched from an argv list to `shell=True` with unquoted interpolation of `upload_dir`, `name`, and `oid`.

## Narrative

ImageMagick 7 policy/delegate behavior does not require a shell. `subprocess.run([...], shell=False)` still execs `/usr/bin/convert` directly and honors the same process environment and policy.xml. The previous argv form was the correct boundary.

With `shell=True`, any metacharacters in the three interpolated values become shell syntax. Even if `name` were constrained upstream by an `ALLOWED_FILES` regex (the comment that documented that assumption was removed, and no such validator exists in this tree), `upload_dir` and `oid` remain fully attacker-shaped once they reach this helper. A value such as metacharacters in `name` or `oid` runs arbitrary commands as the service user and can overwrite paths under `/srv/thumbs/`.

Secondary issue on the same hunk: dropping the absolute `/usr/bin/convert` path for a bare `convert` makes the call PATH-dependent on the runner.

## Release decision

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The patch replaces a safe argv-list `subprocess.run` with `shell=True` and an f-string that interpolates `upload_dir`, `name`, and `oid` into the shell command, enabling command injection. That matches the claimed critical security defect.
